prepared_template.title: Severe apathy despite biochemical improvement in thyroid function
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review: the facts below were documented at different times and are presented together for assessment at the chosen decision point (after thyroid treatment, empirical corticosteroids and brain imaging, but before any CSF drainage procedure). No single pretreatment time point is implied, and later responses are not available at this point.

Patient and course: A woman in her 60s with no relevant medical history developed progressive apathy over a 2-year period, having previously lived independently and remained employed until symptom onset. She eventually became largely bedbound with markedly reduced oral intake requiring enteral feeding.

Examination findings at presentation: severe apathy, general fatigue and constipation. Urinary incontinence was absent. No frontal release signs (grasp, snout), no rigidity, tremor or clinical parkinsonism; eye movements and other reflexes were normal. Profound loss of initiation prevented reliable formal gait assessment. The admission modified Rankin Scale score was 5. There was no history of seizures, impaired consciousness or a fluctuating encephalopathic course.

Thyroid tests and treatment: initial TSH 10.8 mIU/L, free T4 11.2 pmol/L (0.87 ng/dL), thyroid peroxidase antibodies 442 IU/mL and thyroglobulin antibodies 691 IU/mL. Levothyroxine was started at 25 μg/day. Two months later TSH had fallen to 5.4 mIU/L and free T4 risen to 21.8 pmol/L (1.69 ng/dL), but the neurological symptoms were unchanged.

Recorded working diagnoses at this stage: hypothyroidism was initially considered because of fatigue, constipation and the thyroid results; persistent severe impairment despite biochemical improvement prompted investigation of an additional neurological cause. Persistent severe neuropsychiatric symptoms with positive thyroid autoantibodies also prompted consideration of possible thyroid-associated autoimmune encephalopathy, and an empirical course of methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) produced no clear improvement in apathy or functional status. Anti-NAE antibody testing was negative, with results available after the corticosteroid course. These remain provisional, documented hypotheses, not confirmed diagnoses.

Imaging: brain CT showed progressive ventriculomegaly compared with imaging 4 years earlier; the Evans index increased from 0.252 to 0.325 and the callosal angle decreased from 104.6° to 67.6°, with a disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) pattern. Brain MRI confirmed ventriculomegaly with no abnormal DWI hyperintensity or other significant findings beyond the hydrocephalic changes. The clinical history and imaging revealed no antecedent cause of secondary hydrocephalus.

Cognition and behavioural ratings available at this point: the MMSE score before the tap test was 5/30. Retrospectively reconstructed family ratings of the preoperative state (obtained later and therefore susceptible to recall bias) gave an NPI apathy/indifference domain score of 12 (frequency 4 × severity 3), an NPI depression/dysphoria domain score of 0, and an AES-I-J total score of 57 (range 18–72, higher indicating greater apathy).

Documented differential considerations recorded around this assessment, without a confirmed cause: an autoimmune encephalitic process was considered less likely given the slowly progressive 2-year course without seizures or fluctuating consciousness, unremarkable routine CSF findings and absence of additional MRI abnormalities; the negative anti-NAE result was not used to exclude Hashimoto encephalopathy/SREAT given the limited diagnostic utility of the antibody, and thyroid autoantibody positivity alone does not establish central nervous system autoimmunity. Depression was considered; the predominant behavioural feature was marked reduction in spontaneous goal-directed activity. Neurodegenerative and other frontal-subcortical disorders were also in the differential.

Availability limits at this decision point: gait could not be assessed because of severe apathy — this is an unassessable feature, not a documented absence of gait disturbance. Urinary incontinence was documented as absent. No CSF drainage procedure, drainage response, shunt surgery or post-treatment outcome is available at this point; such data, if any exist, are withheld. Unreported items are unknown, not normal.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The patient is largely bedbound with enteral feeding dependence (mRS 5) and severe cognitive impairment (MMSE 5/30); nutritional support and aspiration/pressure-area safety are ongoing concerns. Answers should not recommend live treatment but may assess the evidence for the documented empirical corticosteroid course and levothyroxine continuation.
